quote: That's really the best spot for solar, and it's gonna be the most cost effective.
stewart_read: Roof-placement objection was answered on its own terms (technical justification) rather than flipped toward the bill-pain motivator.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep may be intentionally building technical credibility first since the prospect is engineering-minded and detail-oriented — answering directly may be the right match for this customer's analytical style.
coaching_implication: With an analytical prospect, technical answers can work, but tying back to 'what's expensive is staying on the current bill' would have shortened the roof debate.

quote: the solar bill that I had was through Sunrun Solar, and the bill was $250 a month.
stewart_read: Prospect discloses a full prior solar ownership history with a named competitor (Sunrun) and a specific failure (bill not eliminated) — rep never asks what happened with that install, why it ended, or how long ago.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep may have judged that probing the failed Sunrun relationship risked reopening a wound better left for the closer to handle with full context.
coaching_implication: This is a goldmine detail for differentiation ('unlike Sunrun, we...') that got answered generically instead of probed — closer should get this in the handoff, and setter should have asked what went wrong.

quote: This is bullshit. This is Virginia. This is what I'm getting used to in Virginia.
stewart_read: Prospect vents real frustration at utility billing opacity; rep acknowledges briefly but doesn't use the moment to anchor the bill-pain-as-motivator.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep did briefly validate ('I've heard quite a few people tell me the same thing') which is adequate rapport, not a miss requiring deeper intervention.
coaching_implication: A stronger move ties the utility's opacity directly to 'this is exactly why customers want off the grid' — reinforcing the sale, not just sympathizing.

quote: about how much is your typical bill with them? $2.41.
stewart_read: Bill amount captured but rep moves straight into bill-document collection without flipping the number into an emotional hook.
alternative_hypothesis: The number itself ($2.41, likely truncated/misheard from a larger figure) may be unreliable data, making a flip risky without a clean anchor.
coaching_implication: Even an imperfect number could have been used ('so every month that's money going to Northneck instead of staying in your pocket') — capture without flip per anchor_use finding.

quote: I think recently, it's a lot of, like, the AI computer centers.
stewart_read: Rep speculates on why utility billing/rates are the way they are (AI data centers driving demand) — tangential technical/market commentary beyond setter scope.
coaching_implication: Minor, but time spent theorizing on utility economics could have redirected faster to the design-appointment ask.

quote: it looks like you are in a good area for solar, so we're off to a good start.
stewart_read: Rep proactively signals a positive fit finding, which helped re-engage the prospect after the tense trust exchange.
coaching_implication: Good move — pairing a positive signal right after resolving friction; worth reinforcing as a pattern to replicate.

quote: now do you have a name of a person that I could expect?
stewart_read: Appointment is booked but never gets the full button-up: no one-hour block stated, no no-driving/computer instruction, no explicit 'is that fair?' handshake — rep leaves it to a follow-up text.
alternative_hypothesis: The verified events show button_up as partial and text-followup promised, so this may be an acceptable compressed close for a call that ran long on objections already.
coaching_implication: Even with a long call, the handshake and time-block framing take 15 seconds and materially affect show rate — should not be skipped for time budget reasons.
